tagline: A road kept narrow, through forest, swamp and glacial hills
intro: Ministerial Road carries Route 110 for six miles between Route 138 and US 1 in South Kingstown. Designated a Rhode Island scenic highway in September 1991, it passes upland forest, wetlands and glacial hills. RIDOT highlights mountain laurel and rhododendron beneath the canopy, with stone walls marking former farmland and pasture. Branches meet overhead along several stretches, and vegetation grows close to the narrow shoulders.

Local opposition to state widening plans led to the Ministerial Road Preservation Association and a design plan adopted by the town council. The campaign shifted state plans from widening to repaving. In 1994, Scenic America named it among the country’s ten most endangered scenic roadways. The 1999 stewardship plan called for protecting the road’s winding, tree-covered character and explicitly opposed tourism promotion. Its design goals included keeping pavement no wider than 25 feet, protecting trees and flowering shrubs beside the road, and fitting future alignment to the existing terrain.

Traveling south from Route 138, the road passes Larkin Pond near its northern end, then enters the Great Swamp. It rises onto Tobey Neck and continues to the higher ground of Tuckertown Four Corners. The southern section turns through hills and valleys before reaching US 1 near Perryville.

moments.title: Larkin Pond
moments.text: Larkin Pond lies directly beside Ministerial Road near its northern end. The 1999 Ministerial Road Stewardship Plan described an undeveloped shoreline, with longer views across the water framed by enclosed stretches of vegetation to the north and south. Near this end of the road, the abandoned Narragansett Pier Railroad also crossed the corridor, making a brief opening in the canopy. The former railroad right-of-way became the William C. O’Neill Bike Path in 2000. The bike path intersects Route 110 along the journey through the Great Swamp; one end is at the West Kingston train station.

moments.title: Great Swamp
moments.text: South of Larkin Pond, Ministerial Road enters the Great Swamp. Here the road becomes flat and straight for about a mile and a quarter. Its raised position gives views above the roadside vegetation into the middle of the swamp’s tree canopy. The 1999 Ministerial Road Stewardship Plan identified this as the corridor’s most densely vegetated stretch. Farther south, the roadway rises onto Tobey Neck, a strip of higher ground extending into the swamp. Elsewhere along the corridor, overhanging branches direct the view ahead rather than to the roadside, enclosing the roadway beneath the trees.

moments.title: Tuckertown Four Corners
moments.text: Tuckertown Four Corners occupies higher ground south of Tobey Neck. The 1999 Ministerial Road Stewardship Plan described a small village with a town recreation park, a Grange and several homes. To the west lies Worden Pond, hidden from Ministerial Road. Beyond this settled middle section, the southern road curves through glacial hills and valleys. RIDOT identifies stone walls along much of Ministerial Road as traces of a landscape once dominated by farmland and pasture. The rough terrain and difficult soils kept housing density low in the southern hills, with homes set back from the curving road.
